intro: Alan Chan plays the Fugue, the second movement of Le Tombeau de Couperin. The movement is a three-voice fugue on a short off-beat subject and is dedicated to the memory of Jean Cruppi.

sections.label: A · Subject entries in three voices
sections.mNote: The short subject enters in each of the three parts.

sections.label: Dev · The voices cross
sections.mNote: Off-beat quavers pass between the piano’s three lines

sections.label: Coda · Slower, into E minor
sections.mNote: The three voices end together on a held chord under a fermata.

cues.title: Opening subject and entries
cues.text: The subject begins after a quaver rest, with short notes, small gaps and accents off the beat. The piano starts pianissimo. Two more voices enter in turn with the same phrase, and the earlier voices continue against each new entry.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Fugue, opening; Piano Practical Editions, bars 1–6, p. 13, shows the rest, off-beat accents and three successive entries. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP560971-PMLP4975-Le_Tombeau_de_Couperin.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Jean Cruppi and his family
cues.text: The Fugue is dedicated to Second Lieutenant Jean Cruppi, who was killed in the First World War. His mother Louise, a pianist and salon hostess, encouraged Ravel’s early work, and his father Jean was a politician. Ravel had dedicated his opera L’Heure espagnole to Louise.
cues.evidence: BnF records the dedication and rank: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. The family and Louise’s support are described by Maureen Buja, Interlude, 12 May 2022: https://interlude.hk/the-dead-are-sad-enough-ravel-le-tombeau-de-couperin/. The parental identities and opera dedication are also given by Apple Music Classical: https://classical.music.apple.com/us/work/maurice-ravel-1875-pp50

cues.title: Three-voice texture
cues.text: The subject’s clipped quavers move between the three parts. A held note in one voice can outlast several notes in another, and the middle voice passes between the pianist’s hands. Ravel writes separate stems and slurs for each line.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Fugue, pp. 7–9; Piano Practical Editions, pp. 13–17, preserves the three independently notated voices and their overlapping phrases.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Orchestration of 1919
cues.text: In 1919 Ravel orchestrated four movements of the suite. He left out the Fugue and the Toccata, which exist only for piano. The Fugue is in three voices, all played by one pianist.
cues.evidence: The 1919 orchestration omits the Fugue and Toccata: https://interlude.hk/the-dead-are-sad-enough-ravel-le-tombeau-de-couperin/. The piano score establishes the three-part writing.

cues.title: Final bars of the Fugue
cues.text: At Meno allegro, then Lent, the quavers of the subject slow down and keep their shape. The voices move closer together and end on an E-minor chord held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Fugue, final page; Piano Practical Editions, bars 58–61, p. 17: Meno allegro, slowing instructions, Lent and the E-minor ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Meno allegro to Lent, closing on E minor
transitions.how: At Meno allegro the piano returns to pianissimo and keeps the subject’s off-beat quavers. The tempo slows further to Lent, and the three lines close on E minor. The last bass E and the upper notes are held under fermatas.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Fugue, p. 9; Piano Practical Editions, bars 58–61, p. 17.

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
